prompt: In a chemical equation, what does the double harpoon ⇌ show that a single arrow → does not?

choices.text: The reaction runs in both directions
The reaction runs to completion
choices.why: That is what a single arrow suggests, for an irreversible reaction. The ⇌ shows that products also turn back into reactants.

choices.text: The two sides are resonance structures
choices.why: Resonance is shown with the double-headed arrow ↔, which the section warns not to confuse with ⇌.

choices.text: The reaction is very fast
choices.why: Neither arrow says anything about speed. The ⇌ marks a reversible reaction, one that goes both ways.

explanation: A single arrow → marks an irreversible reaction, which runs one way only. The harpoons ⇌ mark a reversible reaction, in which reactants form products while products re-form reactants, as in N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2.

prompt: In 1803, Claude Louis Berthollet introduced the idea of reversible reactions. What observation led him to it?

choices.text: Sodium carbonate forming around salt lakes
Calcium carbonate dissolving in rainwater
choices.why: That is not in the account. Berthollet saw sodium carbonate forming at the edges of salt lakes, the reverse of a reaction he knew.

choices.text: Iron rusting and then turning back to iron
choices.why: Rust does not turn back into iron on its own. Berthollet's clue was sodium carbonate forming around salt lakes.

choices.text: Water splitting into hydrogen and oxygen
choices.why: That is not what he saw. He noticed sodium carbonate forming around salt lakes, the reverse of a reaction he knew.

explanation: He knew that sodium carbonate and calcium chloride react to give calcium carbonate and sodium chloride. Finding sodium carbonate around the edges of salt lakes, where much salt met calcium carbonate, showed him that the reverse reaction also happens.

prompt: According to the section, what makes a reaction irreversible?

choices.text: Its products can't turn back into reactants
It gives off a lot of heat as it proceeds
choices.why: Giving off heat doesn't make a reaction one-way. An irreversible reaction is one whose products can't turn back into the reactants.

choices.text: It can only take place in a closed system
choices.why: The section's reversible reactions happen in closed systems. Irreversibility means the products can't re-form the reactants.

choices.text: Its reactants and products are all gases
choices.why: The physical state doesn't decide it. What matters is that the products can't convert back to the reactants.

explanation: Irreversible reactions run one way: reactants become products that can't convert back. The section likens this to baking a cake, which can't be turned back into eggs and flour.

prompt: The section's example of an irreversible reaction is combustion, in which a hydrocarbon burns in O2 to give CO2 and H2O. Why doesn't it run backward?

choices.text: CO2 and H2O are stable and don't react back
The products escape as gases into the air
choices.why: The section's reason is chemical: CO2 and H2O are stable and don't react with each other to re-form the hydrocarbon and O2.

choices.text: Combustion is too fast to be reversed
choices.why: Speed doesn't decide whether a reaction can reverse. CO2 and H2O are stable and don't react to give back the reactants.

choices.text: All of the O2 is used up in burning
choices.why: Using up O2 would stop the forward reaction, not explain the lack of a reverse one. The products, CO2 and H2O, are stable and don't react together.

explanation: Water and carbon dioxide are stable, so they don't react with each other to form the hydrocarbon and oxygen again. With no reverse reaction, combustion runs in one direction only.

prompt: What does the section say happens to the reactants and products of a reversible reaction?

choices.text: Neither is ever fully used up
The reactants are used up, then the products revert
choices.why: The two reactions run at the same time, not one after the other. Reactants and products keep reacting and being produced.

choices.text: Only the reactants keep reacting
choices.why: The products react too, giving back reactants. That is what makes the reaction reversible.

choices.text: The products are all used up in the end
choices.why: The products keep forming as well as reacting, so they are never all used up. Neither are the reactants.

explanation: In a reversible reaction the reactants and products are each constantly reacting and being produced. The forward and reverse reactions run at the same time, so neither side is ever fully consumed.

prompt: The section writes A + B ⇌ C + D with rate constants k_1 and k_(−1), as two reactions: A + B → C + D (k_1) and C + D → A + B (k_(−1)). What does k_(−1) describe?

choices.text: The rate constant of C + D → A + B
The rate constant of A + B → C + D
choices.why: That forward reaction has k_1. The subscript −1 marks the reverse reaction, C + D → A + B.

choices.text: A rate constant with a negative value
choices.why: The −1 is only a label for the reverse step. Rate constants are positive numbers.

choices.text: The equilibrium constant of the reaction
choices.why: k_(−1) is the rate constant of one step, the reverse one. An equilibrium constant is a different quantity.

explanation: The reversible reaction is split into a forward reaction with rate constant k_1 and a reverse reaction with rate constant k_(−1). The two run at the same time, products re-forming reactants while reactants form products.

prompt: According to the section, what breaks product molecules apart in a closed system so that they can re-form the reactants?

choices.text: Collisions that supply enough energy
Light absorbed by the products
choices.why: The section doesn't call for light. Molecules colliding with each other supply enough energy to break the products' bonds.

choices.text: The products falling apart on their own
choices.why: The section puts it down to collisions: when molecules collide they can supply the energy to break the products' bonds.

choices.text: Removal of the products from the system
choices.why: Removing products would stop the reverse reaction, not cause it. Collisions with enough energy break the products apart.

explanation: Collisions between molecules cause the reactions in a closed system, in both directions. Once products form, collisions can supply enough energy to break their bonds, giving back the reactants.

prompt: In the section's ballroom picture, girls (reactant A) and boys (reactant B) pair up on the dance floor to form the product. What does a pair breaking up and returning to the sidelines stand for?

choices.text: The reverse reaction, product to reactants
The forward reaction, reactants to product
choices.why: Pairing up on the floor is the forward reaction. A pair leaving the floor turns product back into reactants.

choices.text: An irreversible step in the reaction
choices.why: A break-up shows the product turning back into reactants, which is exactly what an irreversible reaction can't do.

choices.text: The whole reaction coming to a stop
choices.why: The dancing never stops; pairs keep forming and breaking up. A break-up is the reverse reaction.

explanation: Pairs form and break up over and over, just as the forward and reverse reactions both keep running. A pair leaving the floor is the product splitting back into reactants A and B.

prompt: At dynamic equilibrium, what are the forward and reverse reactions doing?

choices.text: Both go on, at equal rates
Both have stopped
choices.why: At equilibrium the reactions keep going; the amounts stay constant only because the two rates match.

choices.text: Both go on, the forward one faster
choices.why: If the forward reaction were faster, products would keep building up. At equilibrium the two rates are equal.

choices.text: Only the reverse reaction goes on
choices.why: Then reactants would keep building up. At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate.

explanation: If the reactants are formed at the same rate as the products, a dynamic equilibrium exists. Molecules keep reacting both ways, but the amounts of reactants and products no longer change.

prompt: The section likens dynamic equilibrium to a water tank that is filled at the same rate as water leaves through a hole. In this picture, what stands for the unchanging equilibrium concentrations?

choices.text: The steady amount of water in the tank
The water steadily flowing into the tank
choices.why: The inflow stands for one of the two reactions, still running. What stays constant, like the concentrations, is the amount of water held.

choices.text: The water steadily leaking out of the hole
choices.why: The outflow stands for one of the two reactions, still running. The constant amount of water held stands for the concentrations.

choices.text: The size of the hole in the side of the tank
choices.why: The hole sets how fast water leaves, more like a rate constant. The concentrations correspond to the amount of water the tank holds.

explanation: Water keeps flowing in and out, just as the forward and reverse reactions keep running. Because the two flows are equal, the amount in the tank stays the same, like the concentrations at equilibrium.

prompt: In the section's biology example, where does hemoglobin pick up oxygen, and where does it release it?

choices.text: Picks it up in the lungs; releases it at capillaries
Picks it up at capillaries; releases it in the lungs
choices.why: That is the wrong way round. Blood takes up oxygen in the alveoli of the lungs and drops it off at the capillaries for the organs.

choices.text: Picks it up in the heart; releases it in the lungs
choices.why: The section names the alveoli of the lungs as where oxygen is picked up. It is released at the capillaries of the body.

choices.text: Picks it up in the lungs; never releases it
choices.why: If hemoglobin never let oxygen go, the organs would get none. It releases oxygen at the capillaries and then picks up CO2.

explanation: As blood passes the alveoli of the lungs, hemoglobin, which has four binding sites, binds oxygen. It drops the oxygen off at the capillaries for the organs and then picks up carbon dioxide.

prompt: Why does the section compare hemoglobin's binding of O2 and CO2 in the body to a reversible reaction?

choices.text: Some bind gas while others release it
Hemoglobin binds only O2, never CO2
choices.why: The section says hemoglobin binds either O2 or CO2. Some molecules are always binding while others are releasing.

choices.text: Hemoglobin is used up as it binds O2
choices.why: Hemoglobin is not consumed; it binds and releases again and again. At any moment some molecules bind while others release.

choices.text: Each molecule binds once and never lets go
choices.why: That would make it one-way, like an irreversible reaction. Hemoglobin keeps binding and releasing O2 and CO2.

explanation: Throughout the body some hemoglobin molecules are picking up or releasing O2 while others pick up or release CO2. So at any moment some reactants are becoming products while some products become reactants again, as in a reversible reaction.

prompt: For A ⇌ B, the forward rate is k_f[A] and the reverse rate is k_r[B]. At equilibrium the two rates are equal. What is the ratio [B]_eq/[A]_eq?

choices.text: k_f/k_r
k_r/k_f
choices.why: The ratio is upside down. From k_f[A]_eq = k_r[B]_eq, dividing both sides by k_r[A]_eq gives [B]_eq/[A]_eq = k_f/k_r.

choices.text: k_f + k_r
choices.why: The sum k_f + k_r governs how fast equilibrium is approached, not where it lies. Equal rates give [B]_eq/[A]_eq = k_f/k_r.

choices.text: 1, since the rates are equal
choices.why: Equal rates don't mean equal amounts. k_f[A]_eq = k_r[B]_eq, so [B]_eq/[A]_eq = k_f/k_r, which is 1 only if k_f = k_r.

explanation: Setting k_f[A]_eq = k_r[B]_eq gives [B]_eq/[A]_eq = k_f/k_r. This ratio is the equilibrium constant K, which ties the position of equilibrium to the two rate constants.

prompt: For A ⇌ B, K = [B]_eq/[A]_eq = k_f/k_r. If k_f is a thousand times larger than k_r, what does the equilibrium mixture look like?

choices.text: Mostly B, with a little A left
Mostly A, with only a little B
choices.why: That would need k_r much larger than k_f. Here K = 1000, so B outnumbers A a thousandfold.

choices.text: Equal amounts of A and B
choices.why: Equal amounts need K = 1, that is, k_f = k_r. Here K = 1000.

choices.text: Only B, with no A at all
choices.why: In a reversible reaction neither side is fully used up. With K = 1000 a small amount of A remains.

explanation: K = k_f/k_r = 1000, so at equilibrium [B] is a thousand times [A]. The reverse reaction still runs, so some A always remains.

prompt: For A ⇌ B starting from pure A, the distance from equilibrium shrinks as exp(−(k_f + k_r)t). Compared with an irreversible A → B with the same k_f, how quickly is the final state approached?

choices.text: Faster, since k_f + k_r is larger than k_f
Slower, since B keeps turning back into A
choices.why: The reverse reaction means less B at the end, but that end is reached sooner. The rate constant of the approach is k_f + k_r, larger than k_f.

choices.text: At the same speed, since only A is there at first
choices.why: B forms at once and starts reacting back, so k_r matters from the start. The approach goes with k_f + k_r.

choices.text: Exactly half as fast, as two reactions compete
choices.why: Nothing halves the approach. The two rate constants add, so the approach, with k_f + k_r, is faster.

explanation: From pure A, B forms and at once starts reacting back, so both rate constants act. The distance from equilibrium shrinks with rate constant k_f + k_r, larger than k_f alone, so the mixture settles sooner, though less B forms than in an irreversible reaction.

prompt: For A ⇌ B, the forward rate constant is k_f = 0.60 s^−1 and the reverse one is k_r = 0.15 s^−1. Using K = k_f/k_r, what is the equilibrium constant K?
explanation: K = (0.60 s^−1)/(0.15 s^−1) = 4.0. The units cancel, and at equilibrium [B] is four times [A].

prompt: A ⇌ B has K = 20 and a forward rate constant k_f = 1.0 × 10^3 s^−1. Using K = k_f/k_r, what is the reverse rate constant k_r, in s^−1?
explanation: k_r = k_f/K = (1.0 × 10^3 s^−1)/20 = 50 s^−1. Since K > 1, the reverse rate constant must be smaller than the forward one, as it is.

prompt: For A ⇌ B starting from pure A, [A] approaches its equilibrium value with an observed rate constant k_obs = k_f + k_r. What is k_obs, in s^−1, when k_f = 0.30 s^−1 and k_r = 0.10 s^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: k_obs = 0.30 s^−1 + 0.10 s^−1 = 0.40 s^−1. The approach is faster than the 0.30 s^−1 of the forward reaction alone, because the reverse reaction also pulls the mixture toward equilibrium.

prompt: For A ⇌ B starting from pure A, the fraction of the material present as B at equilibrium is k_f/(k_f + k_r). What is this fraction when k_f = 3.0 s^−1 and k_r = 1.0 s^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: k_f/(k_f + k_r) = (3.0 s^−1)/(4.0 s^−1) = 0.75, so three-quarters ends up as B and one-quarter stays as A. This matches K = k_f/k_r = 3.0, since 0.75/0.25 = 3.0.

prompt: A ⇌ B starts with [A]_0 = 0.90 M and no B, and K = [B]_eq/[A]_eq = 2.0. Since [A]_eq + [B]_eq = [A]_0, the equilibrium concentration of A is [A]_eq = ([A]_0)/(1 + K). What is [A]_eq, in M? (Give it as a decimal.)
For A ⇌ B at equilibrium, [A]_eq = 0.20 M and k_f = 0.50 s^−1. The forward and reverse rates are equal at equilibrium. What is the reverse rate, k_r[B]_eq, in M/s? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: The forward rate is k_f[A]_eq = 0.50 s^−1 × 0.20 M = 0.10 M/s, and at dynamic equilibrium the reverse rate equals it. Both reactions keep running at 0.10 M/s, so the concentrations don't change.
